# Learning components {#sec-learning-components}

Technical instruction benefits from a predictable learning contract without
turning every book into a course. These blocks state what a reader can do,
what the section assumes, how demanding it is, what was established, and how
to check understanding. Their visible headings carry meaning in every output;
color and layout are only reinforcement.

::: {#obj-threshold-reasoning .learning-objectives}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Learning objectives

After completing this specimen, a reader can:

- distinguish an observable threshold from an inferred design value;
- calculate a bounded operating interval from a nominal value and tolerance;
- record evidence that another reader can independently review.
:::
:::

::: {#pre-threshold-reasoning .learning-prerequisites}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Prerequisites

The reader should be comfortable with arithmetic percentages, voltage units,
and the difference between a measurement and a prediction. No laboratory
equipment is required for the review question.
:::
:::

::: {#plan-threshold-reasoning .learning-plan expected-time="20 minutes" difficulty="foundational"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Study plan

**Expected time:** 20 minutes

**Difficulty:** Foundational
:::
:::

## Guided reasoning {#sec-learning-guided-reasoning}

A nominal 3.3 V signal with a tolerance of 5% has a permitted deviation of
[$3.3 \times 0.05 = 0.165\,\mathrm{V}$]{.alkahest-math-alt alt="three point three times zero point zero five equals zero point one six five volts"}. Its acceptable interval is therefore
3.135 V through 3.465 V. That calculation predicts a range; it does not prove
that a particular circuit stays inside it. Recorded measurements provide the
evidence needed to make that claim.

::: {#sum-threshold-reasoning .learning-summary}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Summary

A tolerance defines a bounded interval around a nominal value. Keep calculated
limits distinct from observations, retain units and conditions with every
reading, and phrase conclusions no more strongly than the evidence permits.
:::
:::

::: {#rev-threshold-reasoning .review-question answer="private"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Review question: threshold evidence

A design predicts a 2.50 V output with a tolerance of 4%. Calculate the
acceptable interval. Then name the additional evidence required before stating
that a built device satisfies the design.
:::
:::

::: {#hint-threshold-reasoning .question-hint data-for="rev-threshold-reasoning"}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Hint

First calculate 4% of 2.50 V. For the second part, distinguish a numerical
prediction from observations made under stated conditions.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-learning-interval}
## Operating-interval exercise

A 5.0 V rail permits a 2% deviation. Calculate its lower and upper limits.
:::

::: {#sol-learning-interval data-for="exr-learning-interval"}
## Operating-interval exercise

Two percent of 5.0 V is 0.1 V, so the permitted interval is 4.9 V through
5.1 V.
:::

The private edition pairs the review question with a separately staged answer
key. Public books retain the question and optional hint without embedding or
merely hiding private answer material.
